task.title: Relics: ship default spec and plan schemas
task.description:
A relic is a new kind of record in Workbook, separate from tasks. It holds specs, plans, decisions, transcripts and similar material, with the same history and sharing that tasks have. A relic has a title, a type, an author, links, and content made of named parts.

Projects can define their own relic schemas, but a new project should not have to. This story ships opinionated default schemas for specs and plans, plus default relationship names for links. The defaults are the shapes we use for Workbook's own specs and plans while building relics, starting with the relic design itself.

## What this delivers

- Built-in schemas for the types `spec` and `plan`.
- A default list of relationship names that every project has.
- The design relic moved onto the default `spec` schema.
- Guidelines and skill that teach agents to write a spec or a plan as a relic.

## How the defaults reach a project

- They are built into Workbook, the way the default statuses are. A new project and a project that just upgraded both have them with nothing to set up, and nobody has to write them into the shared settings.
- A project that saves its own schema for `spec` or `plan` takes over from the default for that type.
- Each released default has a fixed version name and never changes. A later Workbook release can add a newer default beside it. A relic written under a default names that version, as it would for a project schema.
- The naming must make it impossible for a built-in version and a project's own version of the same type to be confused.

## Starting content

This is the starting point. Settle the final content by using it on the design relic and on this story's own plan, then show Dylan the result before it ships, because a released default can never change.

| Type | Properties | Part types |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `spec` | `status`: draft, approved or superseded | `section` (a heading and a body), `decision` (a question, what was chosen, and a body for the reasoning), `open-question` (a question and a body) |
| `plan` | `status`: draft, approved, in progress or done | `section` (a heading and a body), `step` (a title, the steps it needs first, and a body). A step links to the task that builds it. |

## Default relationship names

| Name | Read as |
| --- | --- |
| `implemented-by` | This part of a spec or plan is built by that task. |
| `derived-from` | This was drawn from that source. |
| `summarizes` | This is a summary of that. |
| `decided-in` | This decision was made in that meeting or transcript turn. |
| `changes` | This decision changes that part of a spec. |
| `supersedes` | This relic replaces that one. |
| `relates-to` | A general connection with no stronger meaning. |

- From this story on, a new link's relationship name must be in the default list or in the project's schema. Links made earlier with other names stay readable.
- A project's schema can add names. It cannot remove a default.

## Done when

- A brand new project and an upgraded project can both create a `spec` and a `plan` that are checked against the defaults, with no setup step.
- A project that saves its own `spec` schema is checked against its own from then on.
- The design relic conforms to the default `spec` schema.
- An agent given only the generated guidelines writes a conforming spec and plan.
- The reference documents both defaults and the relationship names.

## Where the design is

The approved design is "Workbook Relics Design" (2026-11-21). It is kept out of the repository. Until "Relics: teach agents to use relics and store the design as the first relic" is done, an untracked copy sits at `specs/2026-11-21-relics-design.html` in Dylan's checkout. After that, read the relic. This description carries what the story needs, and the design wins where the two disagree.
